## Objectives

- See what Module 2 adds to Module 1, and why it comes second
- Speak both dialects, the statistician's and the machine learner's — and see how they led to AI
- State the unsupervised problem precisely — and see why it is harder to grade
- Tell a database from a dataset, and read a dataset's size, types and scale
- Work inside an RStudio project, and know where R is looking for your files
- Check that R, RStudio and the course packages run on your machine

## [Section 1]{.section-kicker} Where we are {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Module 1 gave you a target

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Every method so far had a $y$
:::

- Regression: a number to predict — sales, length of stay, cost
- Logistic and Poisson: a class or a count
- Time series: tomorrow, from yesterday
- Ridge, LASSO: the same, with too many predictors

In every case the data came with **the answer attached**. The model's job was to reproduce it.

## Module 2 takes the target away — then gives it back

| Weeks | Question | Has a $y$? |
|---|---|---|
| 1–3 | *Which customers resemble each other?* — clustering, PCA, correspondence analysis | **No** |
| 4–6 | *Which will churn, default, be readmitted?* — trees, forests, boosting, neural networks | Yes |
| 7 | *Why did the model say that, and how do I tell the board?* | — |

The second half is supervised, like Module 1 — with **algorithms** in place of **equations**.

## [Section 2]{.section-kicker} Two dialects, one subject {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## The same things, with different names

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Machine learning grew up next door to statistics and renamed the furniture
:::

| Statistics | Machine learning |
|---|---|
| Explanatory variable | **Input**, feature |
| Response variable | **Output**, target, label |
| Observations | **Training set** |
| Estimation, fitting | **Training** the model |
| Intercept | **Bias** |
| Transformation | **Activation function** |
| Coefficients, parameters | **Weights** |

You will hear both in this room. They are the same objects.

## Statistics, then machine learning, then AI

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Three generations, asked the same four questions

Each column is built on the one before. This module: the first two.

## Prediction is not inference — a manager's version

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Same model, two different questions
:::

- **Inference**: *does a loyalty card increase spend, and by how much?* — you need a coefficient you can trust, with an interval around it
- **Prediction**: *which of these 40 000 customers will spend most next quarter?* — you need a ranking that holds up, and you do not care why

Module 1 was mostly the first question. Module 2 is mostly the second. Confusing them is the most common analytical mistake in business, and the most expensive.

## [Section 3]{.section-kicker} The unsupervised problem {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## No label, no error, no "correct"

::: {.subtitle-frame}
The problem stated plainly
:::

You have $n$ rows and $p$ columns — customers and their behaviour, patients and their measurements — and **nothing to predict**.

You are asked: is there *structure*? Do these rows fall into groups? Can $p$ columns be summarised by fewer?

- In supervised learning, a wrong prediction is a visible number: $y - \hat y$
- In unsupervised learning there is no $y$. **No residual, no accuracy, no test set.**
- Two analysts can produce two different segmentations of the same customers, and neither is *wrong*

## Then how do you judge it?

- **Internal coherence**: are the groups tight and far apart? (numbers exist — we will use them — but they measure geometry, not truth)
- **Stability**: does the structure survive a different sample, a different seed, a different $k$?
- **Usefulness**: can marketing *act* on the segments? Do clinicians *recognise* the patient groups?

::: {.callout-note}
That last criterion is not a soft one. A segmentation nobody can act on is a wrong segmentation, however tight its clusters.
:::

## The three tools of the next three weeks

| Tool | Question it answers | Business example |
|---|---|---|
| **Clustering** (k-means, hierarchical) | Which rows are alike? | Customer segments; patient case-mix groups |
| **Principal components** | Which few directions carry most of the variation? | The two or three drivers behind twenty survey items |
| **Correspondence analysis** | How do two categorical variables relate? | Brands × attributes — the perception map |

All three are *descriptive*. They organise data; they do not predict anything. That is their strength and their limit.

## Every unsupervised method is a choice you make.  {.statement}

[What counts as "similar" is decided by you, not by the data.]{.muted}

## Three habits, from today

| Do | Don't |
|---|---|
| One project per course: `sbd_26_27` | Loose scripts on the Desktop |
| Data in `data/`, read with `here("data", "file.csv")` | `setwd("C:/Users/anna/Desktop/...")` — a path that exists on one computer on Earth |
| Open the project first, then the script | Open a `.R` file by double-clicking it: R starts in the wrong folder |

[The exam machines are not your laptop. A project plus `here()` is why your script will still run there.]{.muted}

## Script or console?

| Console | Script |
|---|---|
| type a line, Enter, see the answer | write lines in a file, run them when you choose |
| gone when you close RStudio | saved, rerunnable, shareable |
| for *trying* something | for *keeping* something |

Habit to build this week: **everything that matters goes in the script**. The console is a scratchpad. `Cmd/Ctrl + Enter` runs the line your cursor is on; `Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + Enter` runs the whole script.

## Notebook or script?

You will meet both.

- A **script** (`.R`) is code, top to bottom. What we use in class, in labs, and in the exam.
- A **notebook** (`.qmd`, `.Rmd`, Jupyter) mixes text and code cells with their output, in one document. Good for a report; the course site's slides are one.
- Same language inside. The notebook adds prose and layout around the code; it does not change what the code does.

Start with scripts. The notebook is a second thing to learn once the first is comfortable.

## Reading an error without panic

```{.r}
> library(tidyvers)
Error in library(tidyvers) : there is no package called 'tidyvers'
```

- **Read the last line first.** It names the problem: *no package called `tidyvers`*.
- **Find your typo, or your missing step.** Here: a letter. Often: you loaded before installing, or the file is not where you think.
- **Copy the exact message** into a search — or, this year, into an assistant. Then check the answer against what you know.

::: {.callout-important title="Attention"}
Red text in the console is R talking to you, not R breaking. A *warning* lets the code run and tells you something odd happened. An *error* stops it. Learn which one you got before you do anything.
:::

## Five words you will hear all semester

| Word | What it is | You will see it as |
|---|---|---|
| **object** | anything with a name: a number, a table, a model | `fit`, `cust`, `X` |
| **function** | a verb: takes inputs, returns an output | `kmeans(X, 4)` |
| **argument** | an input to a function | `centers = 4` |
| **package** | someone else's functions, installed once, loaded per session | `library(tidyverse)` |
| **data frame** | a table: rows are cases, columns are variables | `cust` from `read_csv()` |

Everything on this slide you will use on Tuesday. Nothing else about programming is required before then.

## [Section 5]{.section-kicker} From a database to a dataset {.section-slide background-color="#002f57"}

## Database ≠ dataset [😡]{.angry}

::: {.subtitle-frame}
Three different objects. Mix them up and you will see this face again
:::

| | Database | Dataset | Data frame |
|--|--------|--------|--------|
| **What** | linked tables, always changing | one table, one question, frozen | the dataset, inside R |
| **Lives** | on a server, behind SQL | in a file: `customers.csv` | in the Environment pane |
| **Example** | the bank's core system | 40 000 customers × 12 columns | `cust` |

[database]{.navy} → *query* → [dataset]{.navy} → `read_csv()` → [data frame]{.navy}

You never analyse a database. You analyse a dataset someone extracted from it — and **which rows, dates and columns they took was already a choice**.

## How big is big data?

::: {.subtitle-frame}
A dataset can grow in two directions, and each breaks something different
:::

<div class="viz">
<svg viewBox="0 0 1100 300" style="max-width:1000px" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Libre Franklin, sans-serif" font-size="19" fill="#1c2226">
  <rect x="40" y="20" width="70" height="260" fill="#002f57" opacity=".85"/>
  <text x="75" y="12" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f6b75" font-size="15">p</text>
  <text x="22" y="155" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f6b75" font-size="15">n</text>
  <text x="140" y="60" fill="#002f57" font-size="24" font-weight="700">Many rows: n</text>
  <text x="140" y="94">every card swipe, every web visit</text>
  <text x="140" y="130" fill="#5f6b75">breaks: computation, and the p-value —</text>
  <text x="140" y="156" fill="#5f6b75">with a million rows, everything is "significant"</text>
  <text x="140" y="196" font-weight="600">→ judge models on a test set instead</text>
  <rect x="620" y="110" width="440" height="70" fill="#b8860b" opacity=".85"/>
  <text x="840" y="102" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f6b75" font-size="15">p</text>
  <text x="604" y="150" text-anchor="middle" fill="#5f6b75" font-size="15">n</text>
  <text x="620" y="40" fill="#b8860b" font-size="24" font-weight="700">Many columns: p</text>
  <text x="620" y="74">80 behaviours per customer, 20 000 genes</text>
  <text x="620" y="216" fill="#5f6b75">breaks: distances, coefficients, and the eye —</text>
  <text x="620" y="242" fill="#5f6b75">when p &gt; n, least squares has no single answer</text>
  <text x="620" y="280" font-weight="600">→ fewer columns: LASSO, then PCA in week 2</text>
</svg>
</div>

Big data usually lives in a **database**. What you analyse is still a **dataset** that fits on your laptop.

## Columns have types

| Type | Column | You can… |
|---------|-----------|--------|
| **Numeric**, continuous | `monthly_charge`, `tenure_months` | average, subtract, measure distance |
| **Numeric**, count | `support_calls` | the same, in whole numbers |
| **Categorical**, nominal | `region`, `payment` | count, tabulate; no mean |
| **Categorical**, ordinal | `contract`: month-to-month < … < two-year | rank; gaps not equal |
| **Categorical**, binary | `churn`: yes / no | the target, from week 4 |

The type decides what you may do. `churn.csv`: **7 numeric, 13 categorical** columns — and clustering and PCA want numbers.

## Five lines you need on Tuesday

```{.r}
library(tidyverse)                     # load the toolbox, once per session
cust <- read_csv("customers.csv")      # file → data frame; <- means "call it"
glimpse(cust)                          # every column, its type, first values
cust$monetary                          # one column: data frame $ column name
summary(cust$monetary)                 # a function applied to that column
```

```{.text}
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.
   41.0   267.0   568.0   796.6   991.2  9214.0
```

`<-` gives a name. `$` picks a column. `f(x)` applies a verb. That is most of the grammar.

## Scale decides who is "close"

Two real customers from `customers.csv`, and what their distance is made of:

| Column | Customer A | Customer B | Share of the distance, **raw** | after `scale()` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `recency` (days) | 35 | 251 | 8% | **48%** |
| `frequency` (orders) | 14 | 3 | 0% | **29%** |
| `monetary` (€) | 607 | 1 338 | **92%** | 5% |
| `tenure`, `returns`, `online` | … | … | 0% | 18% |

Raw, the distance *is* spending: euros run into the thousands. After `scale()` every column counts in standard deviations — and A and B differ because **one bought last month, one eight months ago**.

## Train and test, on real customers

```{.r}
churn <- read_csv("churn.csv")          # 7 000 customers, 28.5% churned
set.seed(1)                             # same random split for everyone
idx   <- sample(nrow(churn), 0.7 * nrow(churn))
train <- churn[idx, ]                   # 4 900 rows: the model learns here
test  <- churn[-idx, ]                  # 2 100 rows: locked until the end
```

| | Rows | Churn rate |
|---|---|---|
| `train` | 4 900 | 28.7% |
| `test` | 2 100 | 28.1% |

Same customers, split at random: the two halves look alike. Any gap between the model's score on `train` and on `test` is the model, not the data. **Look at the test set once.**

## Ten minutes, now, on your own machine

Open RStudio, paste into the Console:

```{.r code-line-numbers="1|3-5|7"}
source("https://sbd-26-27.netlify.app/materials/setup.R")

library(tidyverse)
library(cluster)
library(factoextra)

fviz_nbclust(scale(USArrests), kmeans, method = "wss")
```

If a plot appears, you are ready for Tuesday. If not, that is what the next ten minutes and [office hours](../office-hours.html) are for — not Tuesday's lab.

::: {.callout-important title="Before the lab"}
Bring a laptop that runs the line above. Nobody discovers a missing package in a lab; they discover it tonight.
:::

## Already installed? Check, don't reinstall

```{.r}
R.version.string          # needs "R version 4.6" or newer
```

- **R older than 4.6?** Install the new R from CRAN over it. Your scripts survive; your packages do not — the next line puts them back
- **RStudio**: `Help ▸ Check for Updates`. It updates separately from R: updating one never updates the other
- **Then the same line as everyone else.** It installs only what is missing and changes nothing that works — running it twice is harmless:

```{.r}
source("https://sbd-26-27.netlify.app/materials/setup.R")
```

## Mac or Windows: what actually differs

| | Mac | Windows |
|---|---|---|
| Shortcuts | `⌘` | `Ctrl` |
| Settings | `RStudio ▸ Settings` | `Tools ▸ Global Options` |
| Installer trap | **arm64** (M1 on) vs **Intel**: pick right | needs **admin** rights |
| Paths | `/Users/anna/...` | `C:\Users\...`: backslashes break R — use `here()` |
| Quiet killer | iCloud *Desktop* sync | **OneDrive**: setup keeps you out of it |

All the rest is identical. Details and screenshots: the [Setup page](../setup.qmd) — **reread it at home, calmly**.

## Where the switches are

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
![](../images/setup/03_rstudio_preferences_appearance.png){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
`Tools ▸ Global Options` · Mac: `RStudio ▸ Settings`

- **Appearance**: theme, font, zoom. On the desktop app, install *Fira Code* or *JetBrains Mono* for ligatures: `|>` and `<-` become single glyphs
- **Code ▸ Display**: rainbow parentheses, indent guides, highlight function calls
- **Code ▸ Editing**: *Use native pipe operator* — then `⌘/Ctrl ⇧ M` types `|>`
- **Pane Layout**: console on the right, if you prefer a wide editor
:::
::::

## Shortcuts that make you look fluent

| Keys (Windows: `Ctrl` for `⌘`) | Does |
|---|---|
| `⌘ ⏎` | run the line, or the selection |
| `⌥ -` (Windows `Alt -`) | types ` <- ` |
| `⌘ ⇧ M` | types the pipe, ` \|> ` |
| `⌘ ⇧ C` | comment / uncomment the selection |
| `⌘ ⇧ F10` | restart R — the honest test that your script runs from scratch |
| `⌘ ⇧ P` | the command palette: type what you want, RStudio finds it |
| `Tab` | complete a function, a column or a file name |

[Nobody is graded on their theme. But the restart shortcut will save you once before the exam.]{.muted}

## More tricks: writing code

| Keys (Windows: `Ctrl` for `⌘`, `Alt` for `⌥`) | Does |
|---|---|
| `⌥ ↑` / `⌥ ↓` | move the line up or down |
| `⌘ ⌥ ↑` / `⌘ ⌥ ↓` | copy the line above or below |
| `⌘ D` | delete the line |
| `⌥` + drag | rectangular selection: edit ten lines at once |
| `⌘ I` · `⌘ ⇧ A` | re-indent · reformat the selection |
| `⌘ ⌥ ⇧ M` | rename a variable everywhere it appears in the script |
| `Tab` inside `"…"` | completes a file name: no more typos in paths |

## More tricks: finding your way

| Keys | Does |
|---|---|
| `# Load data ----` | four dashes make a **section**; `⌘ ⇧ O` shows the outline |
| `F1` on a function | its help page, without leaving the script |
| `F2` on a function | jumps to where it is defined |
| `Ctrl .` | go to any file or function in the project by name |
| `⌘ ↑` in the Console | your past commands, filtered as you type |
| `View(cust)` | the data frame as a spreadsheet |
| `⌥ ⇧ K` | every shortcut there is |
